parts: Lesson 27: Nuclear Fission and Fusion — Summary

In a nuclear reaction the nuclei of reactants interact to form new nuclei. Charge, nucleon number, momentum and mass-energy are all conserved. Reactions can be triggered by protons, deuterons, neutrons and other light nuclei.
Example: ²⁷Al + ⁴He → ³⁰Si + ¹H, where the emitted particle is a proton.
Reactions can release energy (exothermic) or absorb it (endothermic). The Q-value = (mass of reactants − mass of products) × c².
The neutron is the best projectile because, being neutral, it is not repelled by the nucleus.
A heavy nucleus splits into two medium nuclei with the release of energy and 2–3 neutrons. For example: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + about 200 MeV.
Energy is released because the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon, so there is a loss of mass (E = Δm c²).
U-235 undergoes fission with slow (thermal) neutrons of about 0.025 eV, less than 0.1 eV. Fissile materials are U-235 and Pu-239.
The neutrons released can cause further fissions — a chain reaction. Uncontrolled, it gives an atom bomb; controlled, it runs a nuclear reactor.

Reactor parts: fuel (U-235 or Pu-239); a moderator (heavy water or graphite) that slows neutrons; control rods (cadmium or boron) that absorb extra neutrons to control the rate; a coolant (water, heavy water or liquid sodium) that removes heat to produce steam; and shielding.

Light nuclei fuse into a heavier nucleus with release of energy, e.g. four protons → helium + 2 positrons + about 26.7 MeV. Fusion needs a temperature of about 10⁷ K (thermonuclear), and is the source of the energy of the sun and stars.
Fusion releases more energy per unit mass of fuel than fission and leaves less radioactive waste, but it is hard to control. It is the principle of the hydrogen bomb.
